entry.title: SAP Ariba Invoicing 2605 Release Key Innovations
entry.content:
Hello SAP Ariba Community!  We’re excited to share the latest enhancements in SAP Ariba Invoicing (formally SAP Ariba Central Invoice Management (CIM)) coming in the Q2 2026 release! As part of our ongoing commitment to innovate and streamline invoice management, we’re happy to announce these key enhancements which are designed to simplify the user experience and operations as well as deliver greater efficiencies overall to our customers.  We hope you enjoy these highlights!

1.  Support of Ad Hoc Approvers in the Approval Workflow (CIM-2578)

In Accounts Payable, exceptions are normal. An unexpected requirement such as an urgent quarter-end invoice can require extra eyes. Until now, that often meant stopping and reconfiguring an approval workflow or sending an invoice back to the start.

In this release, we’re introducing an important capability that many of our users have been asking for: the ability to add or remove approvers in SAP Ariba Invoicing to help your teams handle exceptions without slowing down the process. It’s a simple feature that has a big impact on continuity, cycle times, and on the overall user experience.

Support of Ad Hoc Approvers in the Approval Workflow:

  • You can add and remove ad hoc approval steps while a supplier invoice is already in the approval process.
  • Previously, approvers could only be configured before the workflow started in Workflows for Supplier Invoice Approval.
  • You can dynamically add or remove up to 10 additional approval steps during the approval process to address real-time needs and keep work moving.

Invoice approvals rarely follow a perfect script. This enhancement gives AP, procurement, and finance the flexibility to adapt to unexpected situations while maintaining control.

Key business benefits include:

  • Faster cycle times: Handle exceptions in-flight instead of restarting or reconfiguring the workflow. This keeps critical invoices moving and reduces end-of-period bottlenecks.
  • Better control and compliance: Insert the right approvers at the right time for sensitive categories, high-value invoices, or regulatory checks—without bypassing governance.
  • Less rework: Avoid sending invoices back to drafting or re-submitting just to change approvers. Reduce back-and-forth between AP and requesters.
  • Improved collaboration: Bring in subject matter experts or temporary approvers when needed, then remove those steps once the exception is resolved.    

Below is an example to visualize this enhancement:         

2.  Support of Approvers Based on Spend Limits (CIM-3050)

With this feature, you can now add additional approvers to a supplier invoice based on user approval limits. It allows you to automatically escalate supplier invoices to approvers in the approval hierarchy when the invoice gross amount exceeds an approver's defined limit.

How it works at a glance:

  • You define approval limits for users or roles and maintain your approval hierarchy in SAP Ariba Invoicing.
  • When the invoice gross amount exceeds the current approver’s limit, the system automatically adds the next approver(s) in the hierarchy until the right authorization level is reached.
  • The feature augments your existing approval rules to improve coverage without adding complexity for end users.

This feature introduces important benefits and controls:

  • Stronger financial control: Enforce approval policies consistently by making sure invoices are always reviewed by approvers with the appropriate spending authority.
  • Faster cycle times: Reduce back-and-forth and rerouting caused by invoices landing with approvers who don’t have sufficient limits.
  • Improved compliance and auditability: Create a clear, auditable trail that shows why and how an invoice moved up the chain.
  • Scalability as you grow: As organizations change, limits and hierarchies can be updated without reworking every approval flow.

In the screenshot, you can see the new Approvers based on the spend limit field:

3.  Enhancement to Invoice Rejection Reason (CIM- 3439)

With this release, we’ve introduced clearer supplier notifications for invoice rejections in SAP Ariba Invoicing.  Exception handling is part of every accounts payable operation. When you need to reject an invoice, it should be clear who gets notified and easy to prove that the notification went out. With this release, we have made this simpler and more transparent.

What’s new:

  • Enhancement to Invoice Rejection Reason: When you click Reject Invoice, the system now shows the email ID (email address) of the supplier contact who will receive the rejection notification.
  • Automatic confirmation in Comments: After you reject, the invoice’s Comments tab records a system comment that confirms the notification was sent to the supplier, including the supplier’s email ID.

Some key benefits include:

  • Greater transparency: AP analysts see exactly who will be notified before they confirm a rejection.
  • Faster dispute resolution: Clear routing reduces back-and-forth and helps suppliers get the right information the first time.
  • Better accountability: A time-stamped comment creates an audit trail without manual notes.
  • Improved supplier experience: Suppliers get a timely, directed notice and can act faster.

The screenshot below displays the Supplier Email that will be notified of the invoice rejection:

These enhancements are intended to demonstrate SAP's commitment to building solutions that support and enable your business process needs.

Stay tuned for more enhancements in SAP Ariba Invoicing to drive efficiency and flexibility in your business process.

entry.title: SAP AI: Beyond the Hype and Into the Real World
entry.content:
Three days in Excel hell. Twenty supplier bids. One AI agent that knows your data. This is the SAP AI story your vendor deck won't tell you — first in a series.

I've been on the digital transformation journey for more years than I care to admit. I truly believe that constant evolution is the only way to stay relevant in procurement, but lately, it feels like the word "transformation" has been completely hijacked by a single two-letter acronym: AI. Everywhere I turn, AI is the only topic in the room. It is being pitched as the ultimate cure-all, yet for most of us, the daily reality still involves wrestling with legacy systems and messy data.

After endless conversations about AI's impact today, where it is going, and how it fits into our daily lives, I've realized that what we need is not more noise, but a clear roadmap.

My intention with this series is to provide a solid understanding of where we are today, set some realistic expectations, and point out where the magic really happens when we get it right.

We will look at what SAP is doing broadly with Business AI, while zooming in specifically on the procurement space where the impact is most immediate. Each post in this series will focus on a specific piece of the puzzle or a real-world scenario, helping you not only navigate this AI transformation but ensuring you actually see tangible value at the end of it. And I promise: no marketing fluff and no buzzword bingo.

 

The Anatomy of Success: How the Pieces Actually Fit Together

Stop thinking about AI as a single feature you can switch on. It's a high-performance system built from three distinct, non-negotiable layers. Pull any one out and the whole thing fails to deliver value. Here's the blueprint:

 The three layers of the SAP AI stack. Remove any one and the system fails to deliver value.

Each layer has a clear job. BTP is where your code actually runs and your security lives. SAP Business Data Cloud is the part that prevents your AI from getting confused — it makes sure a "Supplier" in one system is the same thing as a "Vendor" in another. Joule is the conversational front door that takes your natural-language request and orchestrates the work across every back-end system. Everything else in this post depends on these three working together.

 

Four Flavors of SAP AI You'll Actually Encounter

Not all AI is created equal — and you'll meet at least four different flavors in any real SAP deployment. Each one solves a different problem and shows up in your workflow in a different way. Here's how to recognize them:

 Four flavors of SAP AI. Each one solves a different problem — and you'll meet all of them

 

Talk Is Cheap. Let's Look at a Real Scenario.

We've all heard the lofty promises of AI, but talk is notoriously cheap. Instead of another high-level theory, I want to show you a practical scenario that has already been built and is currently saving procurement experts hundreds of hours. This is not some futuristic concept waiting for a release date — it's how we're solving real-world complexity right now.

 The Bid Analysis Agent in action — what 80% of the heavy lifting looks like.

WHAT HAPPENS TODAY WITHOUT AI

You're stuck in Excel hell for three days. You're manually pivoting data, trying to run "what if" scenarios, and likely making a few coffee-fueled typos along the way. By the time you finally have an answer, the market data has already shifted and your analysis is effectively a historical document.

THE BASIC AI EXPERIENCE

You try to use a generic, public AI tool. You upload a spreadsheet and ask for an analysis. It gives you a shallow "cheapest is best" answer, hallucinates a few shipping routes that don't exist, and potentially leaks your sensitive pricing data to the public web. Fast, but dangerous — and completely lacking business context.

THE REALISTIC SAP AI FUTURE

You use a Bid Analysis Agent grounded in your actual Ariba data. You ask Joule to show the award scenario that minimizes risk if fuel prices spike. The agent evaluates the trade-offs, highlights bid outliers, and suggests a data-driven strategy in seconds by factoring in unit prices, shipping, and risk data. You're still the decision-maker — but the AI has handled 80% of the analytical heavy lifting for you.


Straight Talk: Paying the Data Tax

AI in 2026 is not about replacing the procurement professional. It is about capacity. It's about getting that 20% to 30% of your week back from repetitive, manual work.

But let's be real about the Data Tax. I'm not suggesting every organization is starting from scratch. In fact, most customers I talk to have done a great job with their supplier and master data. The real mess usually hides elsewhere: in the offline spreadsheets, the unstructured sourcing history, and the fragmented procurement processes that haven't quite made it into the system yet.

 

Two data realities. One of them turns your AI into a confident liar.

Good data is structured, centralized, and consistent. It means having one version of the truth, so that when you ask an AI for a risk assessment, it isn't hallucinating because it found three different versions of the same contract.

Bad data is the fragmented manual sprawl — the tribal knowledge and the manual workarounds that live outside your digital core.

When you try to use AI with bad data, the implications are simple: the AI becomes "confidently wrong." It will give you an answer, but that answer will be based on a fragment of reality. Paying the Data Tax is not a one-time activity or a weekend cleanup. It's an ongoing evolution in how you store and leverage your information — a commitment to continuous improvement where your AI outputs steadily improve as your data strategy matures.

You simply cannot ignore the data layer of the architecture and expect the interaction layer to give you accurate results.

What's Next

Moving forward, this series will dive deep into the specific AI scenarios and features that drive actual savings in both time and money. I'll be sharing not just what we're building at SAP, but also the real-world best practices I'm seeing from other leading organizations that are successfully closing the "execution gap." There's a wealth of peer knowledge out there that can benefit us all.

I have specific use cases planned, but I'm always interested in your perspective. If there's a particular challenge you're facing or a piece of the puzzle you want to see solved, let me know what you'd like me to cover in future chapters.

entry.title: EDI in the age of agentic AI, the structural mismatch nobody is naming
entry.content:
Somewhere in most people’s houses, there is a road atlas. Beautifully printed, comprehensive, the place you were looking for always on the join between two pages or on the fold where the binding had eaten the postcode. Then the internet arrived and you printed out a route from a website, which was a digital map in name and a dead letter on the passenger seat. The thing that actually changed driving was location services. The moment the map knew where you were and where the closures were, it stopped being an artefact and became a network you could query. Then Waze went further: routing you using information contributed by every other driver on the road. A car on the hard shoulder. A speed camera. A tailback the official feed would not catch for twenty minutes. The map was no longer a thing you read. It was a network where every participant made the whole more intelligent for everyone else.

So, time to drag this back to my actual day job, which is business networks and S/4HANA. Every S/4 programme has to answer a deceptively simple question: how will this enterprise communicate with the outside world once the transformation is done? The old plumbing breaks. IDocs are restructured or retired, partner mappings need re-testing, and on-premises middleware that has quietly carried the business for fifteen years, invisible until the moment it failed, cannot keep up. The bill comes due. But the real choice is not how to fix the plumbing. It is whether the connectivity layer should remain a way of moving documents between two known parties, or become a queryable network that an autonomous agent can reason over. The answer the market is offering, namely modernise the EDI, move it to the cloud, add a bit of AI, is the corporate equivalent of printing out a route from the website. Technically more modern. Functionally the same piece of paper.

Give cloud EDI its due first. Moving an on-premises EDI estate into a managed cloud genuinely helps: better resilience, faster partner onboarding, centralised monitoring, and no more single-point-of-failure when your one EDI specialist retires. I am not arguing against any of it. I am arguing that none of it changes what the architecture is.

Cloud EDI is still EDI. It is still bilateral. It is still static. It produces a dead document, accurate at the moment of transmission, useless the moment anything changes, and it has nothing useful to offer an autonomous agent. Agents do not just process documents after the fact. They need to interrogate live, networked data, who has capacity now, at what price, under what constraints, and EDI has no way of exposing that.

This is the part that needs spelling out. Consider a worked example. A buyer agent at a Tier 1 manufacturer receives an order for three thousand units of a sub-assembly. To place that order well, the agent needs to know which suppliers across the network have capacity, at what price, with what lead time, tariff exposure, and carbon intensity. It needs to consider whether splitting the order across two suppliers reduces risk enough to justify the higher unit price, and whether either supplier is constrained by a Tier 2 component that has gone short this week. I have sat through several of those demos this year. Not one of them could have been accomplished over a one-to-one document pipe. Not one. The agent needs a network where it can ask a question and get an answer that reflects the current state of that network.

The architectural requirement is the same whatever you call it: networked, queryable, shared state across thousands of partners, with event-level visibility and the means to act. SAP Business Network is the specific instantiation of this within the S/4HANA ecosystem. The label matters less than the property. EDI was engineered in the 1970s to do the opposite of all of it.

Watch the market on this one. Read any vendor argument for "modernising your EDI to the cloud" carefully and you will find them describing a system that decouples mapping from the ERP, holds partner profiles centrally, and offers a real-time cockpit across thousands of partners. That is not modernised EDI. That is a network with a different name on the door. The market is quietly building the right thing while loudly selling the wrong word for it.

Two numbers tell you the shape of it. Interos, in its 6 Supply Chain Risks for 2026 report, finds that 90% of organisations remain blind to sub-tier disruptions for up to 48 hours. APQC's 2026 Supply Chain Priorities and Challenges: Cross-Industry Report finds that only one in three organisations have a strategy this year to increase visibility into lower-tier suppliers. Two-thirds are not even planning to do anything about it. One-to-one connections cannot reach those lower tiers. They cannot reach an agentic workflow either.

You already know I work in this space. The companies already on a network are building compound advantage in supplier visibility, agentic readiness, and network intelligence that a one-to-one pipe cannot replicate after the fact.

This should not be a Phase 2 conversation. It should not be kicked to 2028. It should not be left for the next team to discover. By then the programme team has moved on. The decision is business as usual. Nobody around the table remembers it was once a choice. A one-to-one pipe cannot reroute when a supplier fails, recompute when a tariff lands, or answer when an agent asks it a question. A network can do all three. The companies that defer will spend the next three years falling behind quietly, and in an agentic world three years is no longer a planning horizon. It is a generation. Kicking this to 2028 is not a deferral. It is a decision to fall behind, taken by people who will not be there to see it land.

The road atlas works. So does the printed page from the route planner. Neither of them is going to tell you about the lorry on the hard shoulder at the next junction, or that a faster route has just opened up that the rest of your competitors are already taking.

entry.title: 4 Ways CPOs Can Drive Procurement Outcomes with AI
entry.content:
The CPOs I've been talking to are navigating a different kind of pressure than they faced two years ago. It's not just about cost discipline anymore. Tariff volatility is forcing them to review supplier contracts. Over-concentrated supply bases can be exposed overnight by a single geopolitical event. And boards expect measurable AI ROI in weeks, not months. Procurement is being asked to do more with less and to manage more risk with greater precision.

There's no shortage of AI tools promising to help here — but the problem is that most AI in procurement is being deployed as a stand-alone agent or as an automated workflow that operates without visibility into what's happening across the rest of the business.

When sourcing isn't aware of spend insights or supplier-risk signals, you don't get AI-driven procurement, you get AI-assisted silos.

You need Autonomous Spend Management with SAP, which is a connected system where:

  • AI works across the entire source-to-pay process 
  • A supplier risk surfaces immediately in sourcing
  • Compliance requirements are enforced automatically at the point of purchase
  • A category strategy informs every downstream decision.

Autonomous Spend solutions support faster decisions, fewer handoffs, and consistent outcomes at scale — proactively identifying supply risks, optimizing supplier relationships, localizing compliance for invoices and expenses, and uncovering untapped savings opportunities.

What I'm Hearing from CPOs

Over the past few months, I've had the privilege of speaking with procurement leaders across industries and geographies at SAP Sapphire in Orlando and at the Procurement Leaders AI Forum in London, and in a lot of conversations in between. What struck me wasn't any single insight, but rather how consistent the pressure is, regardless of company size or sector.

In Orlando, I spoke to a CPO from a global manufacturer who had just spent three months renegotiating supplier contracts because of tariff changes he hadn't seen coming. A few weeks later in London, I sat down with a procurement transformation lead at a financial institution who was dealing with a completely different set of facts but describing the exact same feeling. The same sense that the ground keeps shifting.

This isn't a moment of isolated disruption. It's a structural shift in what procurement leadership requires.

What This Means for the Function

The questions I’m hearing aren’t 'which tasks can AI handle?' They're 'what does my function become when AI handles these tasks?' That's a much more consequential question.

Most procurement teams today spend the majority of their capacity on coordination: routing approvals, researching suppliers, answering questions although answers already exist somewhere in their systems, and manually connecting information that should already be connected.

When AI begins to execute these routine tasks autonomously — routing, researching, recommending, and enforcing policy — procurement capacity shifts. Your team starts to be seen as strategists. That shift compounds over time: lower cycle times, fewer leakage points, and a function that can respond to a tariff change or a supply disruption in hours rather than weeks.

The four examples below show what this looks like in practice when a procurement organization navigates a major strategic shift. Individually, each story is about a person using AI to work differently. Together, they describe what an elevated function actually looks like.

Kate: AI-Powered Category Management

Kate had her procurement world figured out. She’d spent five years perfecting steel and electronics categories, with color-coded spreadsheets she could navigate in her sleep.

Then her company decided to pivot to electric vehicles and her carefully organized category plans became obsolete overnight.

She needed to quickly build new market intelligence, identify qualified suppliers, and create category frameworks that could adapt as technology evolved.

The traditional category development process wouldn't work while the market was moving this fast.

Fortunately, Kate had Category Management Agents to help her transform her approach. Within days she had access to:

  • Comprehensive 360-degree supplier profiles with continuous updates
  • Strategy recommendations grounded in proven frameworks
  • Real-time risk highlights and market intelligence

Instead of spending weeks researching new components, Kate used AI-driven strategy recommendations to build a new category with intelligent subcategories. She had a complete view of market spend and supplier dynamics in one place, alongside recommendations with risk highlights that helped her make informed decisions.

Expected impact: Reduced maverick spend by 5-15% by aligning demand to category strategy and approved channels.* 

Marcus: Intelligent Sourcing at Scale

Identifying the right strategic category was just the beginning. The pressure had now shifted to Marcus, the sourcing manager.

Marcus knew the drill: RFPs meant late nights, multiple spreadsheets, and that sinking feeling when he realized he'd been researching the wrong supplier for three hours.

Without AI support, it could take him weeks to pull together detailed tech specs, quality certifications, testing protocols, and environmental impact criteria. He was conducting manual research on potential suppliers across fragmented data sources — checking one system for financial stability, another for past performance, and yet another for current capabilities.

With Sourcing Assistant, Marcus started a conversation with Joule and kicked off his RFP with just a few prompts. Joule analyzed his requirements and business objectives, articulated what he needed to source, and eliminated the research and guesswork, delivering:

  • Supplier recommendations based on his unique business environment
  • Draft comprehensive questionnaires
  • Transparent bid analysis with AI-generated counteroffers

Using data already in SAP like past contracts, supplier history, and performance records, Joule made recommendations that were specific to Marcus's business context. 

Expected impact: Improved total cost of ownership by 5-15% through better specifications, supplier selection, and negotiation support.*

Christopher: Streamlined Buying Decisions

With a strong category strategy and sourcing plan in place, value could still leak out — and it often does at the buying stage. Christopher from operations ran into exactly this problem when his team ran low on high-voltage cables for a critical production line.

Without AI guidance, he faced analysis paralysis. Should he order cables with additional wiring harnesses? Which supplier offered the fastest delivery for his specific requirements? Meanwhile the approval process became a bottleneck, bouncing between Finance for budget verification and Procurement for contract compliance.

The Requisition Assistant transformed Christopher's buying experience by:

  • Guiding him automatically to compliant choices
  • Streamlining approvals with pre-populated context
  • Enforcing policy compliance and preventing maverick spending

Instead of getting stuck in technical decisions and approval delays, AI agents guided Christopher to compliant choices by suggesting cables that matched his specs with approved suppliers while routing his requests to the right approvers.

Expected impact: Saved 2-4% through channel consolidation and higher on-contract compliance.* 

Priya: Services Procurement Made Simple

But the complexity didn't end with direct materials. Priya from facilities management needed to secure installation services for the new cables — and procuring services introduced an entirely different set of challenges. She had to draft a comprehensive Statement of Work (SOW) but lacked the expertise to define the requirements clearly and wasn't familiar with the approval workflows.

The Services Procurement Assistant became Priya's expert guide, offering:

  • A simple conversational interface with Joule
  • Comprehensive, AI-generated SOW drafts
  • Automatic routing with proper documentation

She simply told Joule what she needed: installation services for the London facility. Joule confirmed understanding, drafted an SOW with clear terms, milestones, and performance metrics, and automatically routed the request.

Expected impact: Reduced compliance breaches by up to 91% with policy-by-design workflows and standardized SOWs.* 

The procurement function is at an inflection point.

Connected AI enforces policy by design, reducing exceptions without slowing the business. Organizations that connect AI across the entire source-to-pay process are building an advantage that compounds faster responses to supply disruption and greater team capacity for strategic decisions. Organizations that deploy AI in isolated pockets will capture limited value. And the gap between those two outcomes is widening every quarter.

If you want to see what this looks like in practice for your organization, let's talk.

  • Already using SAP Ariba? Contact your Account Executive to learn how you can activate Joule.
  • New to SAP Ariba? Reach out to our team to request a demo.

*Source:  BCG/SAP Study (2026) on agentic AI in spend management. Values based on a net-new €10B company with €5B procurement spend. Value unlock tiers: XL: above €500M, L: €200M–€500M, M: €50M–€200M, S: below €50M. Actual results vary by baseline, category mix, and policy maturity.

entry.title: Locking Alterations to Service Entry Sheets Created via Interface (Ariba and Fieldglass)
entry.content:
Introduction

In a modern source-to-pay landscape, SAP S/4HANA rarely works alone. When external workforce and services procurement is handled in SAP Ariba or SAP Fieldglass, key documents such as the Service Entry Sheet (SES) are created automatically in S/4HANA through a standard integration interface — not by a user sitting in ML81N.

This automation is powerful, but it introduces a governance risk: if a business user manually edits or reverses an interface-created SES inside S/4HANA, the S/4HANA record immediately diverges from the system of record (Ariba or Fieldglass). That drift ripples into goods receipt, invoice verification and financial postings.

In this post I share a clean-driven approach to block manual changes to interface-created SES documents using the standard SAP enhancement MBCF0002 (user exit EXIT_SAPMM07M_001), and I provide the complete ABAP code so you can adapt it to your own landscape.

 

The Problem

  • SES documents for Ariba / Fieldglass POs are generated automatically via interface.
  • Manual modification or reversal in ML81N breaks consistency between S/4HANA and the upstream system.
  • The result: mismatched service entry sheet,incorrect financial postings.

We need a guardrail that allows the interface to keep posting freely, while preventing manual users from tampering with those documents.

Solution Approach

We use the standard SAP User Exit EXIT_SAPMM07M_001, part of enhancement MBCF0002, which is triggered during goods movement processing. Custom validation logic goes into the customer include ZXMBCU02.

The design is deliberately Code driven .A custom table to stores the relevant PO document types for Ariba/Field Glass Interface

Logic flow inside ZXMBCU02

  1. Check the current transaction is manual SES maintenance (SY-TCODE = 'ML81N').
  2. Read PO document type from the custom table.
  3. Retrieve the PO document type (BSART) for the SES line by joining EKPO, EBAN and EKKO on the PO number / item from I_MSEG.
  4. Compare the document type against the configured Fieldglass / Ariba PO types.
  5. If the PO type matches with the one in custom table raise an error and block the change: "Editing Field Glass SES is not allowed".

Custom ABAP Code (Include ZXMBCU02)

 

Conclusion

By combining the standard MBCF0002 enhancement with a small, custom code-driven include, we get a robust guardrail that:

  • Protects data integrity between S/4HANA and Ariba / Fieldglass,
  • Requires no core modification — it is a supported user exit,
  • Leaves the interface untouched, blocking only manual ML81N edits and reversals.

entry.title: SAP Ariba Invoicing 2608 Release Key Innovations
entry.content:
1.  Activity Log Includes Automatic Changes (CIM-1559)

As invoice processes become more automated, transparency becomes even more important. Finance teams need to understand not only what changed on a supplier invoice, but also whether the change was made by a user or automatically by the system.

With this release, SAP Ariba Invoicing introduces an enhancement that helps improve visibility and audit readiness in day-to-day invoice processing.

What's changing?

The activity log in the Manage Supplier Invoices Centrally app now captures automatic system changes alongside manual updates. Until now, you could see when your team adjusted invoices, but system-driven actions stayed hidden behind the scenes.

Why this matters to you

When something changes in your invoice, you need to know what has changed and why. This visibility is critical for several reasons:

  • Audit readiness: You have a complete record of every modification—manual and automatic—making compliance reporting easier
  • Troubleshooting: When an invoice behaves unexpectedly, your team can quickly trace the chain of events to understand what triggered it
  • Team confidence: Your finance and procurement teams gain peace of mind knowing nothing happens without a documented trail
  • Process improvement: By seeing where the system intervenes, you can identify bottlenecks and optimize workflows

How it works

Simply open the activity log in Manage Supplier Invoices Centrally. You'll now see a complete timeline of invoice changes—from validation rules that auto-corrected data to system-initiated status updates. Each entry tells the full story of that invoice's journey.

Business Value

For finance and shared services teams, this update can reduce the time spent investigating invoice changes. Users can now see a more complete activity history directly in the app, without needing to rely on separate checks or additional support.

This is especially valuable in high-volume invoice environments, where automation plays a key role in keeping processes efficient. By making automatic changes visible in the activity log, teams can work with greater clarity and control.

The following types of changes are now displayed in the activity log:

This enhancement reflects our commitment to helping you build more transparent, auditable invoice processes.  Clearer visibility means better control.

2.  Enhancement of Invoice Rejection Email to Support CC (Carbon Copy) Users (CIM- 3438)

In invoice processing, clear and timely communication is essential. When an invoice is rejected, suppliers and internal teams need to understand what happened, why it happened, and who needs to act next.  In this release, we are introducing an enhancement that helps improve transparency and collaboration during the invoice rejection process.

Enhancement of Invoice Rejection Email to Support CC Users

With this enhancement, users can now add additional recipients as CC recipients when sending an invoice rejection email notification.

When rejecting an invoice, the user can select CC recipients from the list of available users. This ensures that the right stakeholders receive a copy of the rejection notification and stay informed without requiring separate follow-up emails.

Why This Matters

Invoice rejections often involve more than one person. For example, procurement, accounts payable, supplier relationship managers, or business owners may need visibility into why an invoice was rejected and what needs to happen next.

Previously, if additional stakeholders needed to be informed, users often had to forward emails manually or send separate messages. This could lead to delays, missed information, or inconsistent communication.

With CC support in invoice rejection emails, teams can now communicate more efficiently directly from the invoice rejection process.

Key Business Benefits

  • Improved transparency
  • Consistent and timely communications
  • Less manual intervention to ensure communications with all key stakeholders

The right stakeholders can be included at the time of rejection, helping everyone stay aligned on invoice status and next steps.

In the Reject Invoice popup, the Additional Email field can be used to add additional recipients for the invoice rejection email:

3.  Level-Based Approval for Supplier Invoice Workflows (CIM- 3451)

Approvals are a critical part of invoice management. They help organizations control spend, reduce risk, and make sure the right people review the right transactions before payment. But as businesses grow, approval needs often become more complex—especially for high-value invoices, sensitive categories, or invoices tied to strategic suppliers.

With the Q3 2026 release of SAP Ariba Invoicing, we are introducing Level-Based Approval for Supplier Invoice Workflows, a new capability designed to help organizations route supplier invoices through additional approval levels based on their management hierarchy.

With this feature, organizations can configure additional approval levels for supplier invoices when specific business conditions are met.

For example, if an invoice exceeds a defined value threshold or is considered business-critical, the system can automatically route it beyond the primary approver to one or more additional managers in sequence. This escalation follows the organization’s management structure, helping ensure that invoices requiring higher authority receive the right level of review before they are approved for payment.

Why This Matters

Many organizations need more than a simple one-step approval process. Certain invoices require added oversight, but manually identifying and escalating them can create delays, inconsistent controls, and extra work for accounts payable teams.  Level-Based Approval helps address these challenges by making invoice routing more structured and automated.

Key benefits include:

  • Stronger financial control
    High-value or sensitive invoices can be routed to approvers with the appropriate authority level.
  • Improved compliance with internal policies
    Approval workflows can better reflect your organization’s delegation of authority and management hierarchy.
  • Reduced manual intervention
    The system automatically determines when additional approval levels are required, helping reduce the need for manual routing or follow-up.
  • Greater consistency in approvals
    Similar invoices can follow the same approval path based on defined conditions, supporting more predictable and auditable processes.
  • Faster, more confident decision-making
    Approvers receive invoices in the right sequence, helping teams avoid confusion around who needs to review and approve next.

How It Works

Organizations can define conditions that determine when additional approval levels are needed. When a supplier invoice meets those conditions, SAP Ariba Invoicing automatically routes the invoice through the configured approval chain.

The approval sequence starts with the primary approver and then moves upward through the required management levels. This helps ensure that each invoice is reviewed by the appropriate people based on its value, risk, or business importance.

For example:

  1. A supplier invoice is submitted.
  2. The invoice meets a defined condition, such as exceeding a certain amount.
  3. The invoice is routed to the primary approver.
  4. After approval, it is routed to the next management level.
  5. The process continues until all required approval levels are completed.

Example Use Cases

This capability can support a range of common invoice approval scenarios, including:

  • Invoices above a specific monetary threshold
  • Invoices related to critical suppliers or projects
  • Invoices that require executive or senior management visibility
  • Invoices tied to specific categories, regions, or business units
  • Exceptions that require additional review before payment

Business Value for Accounts Payable and Procurement Teams

For accounts payable teams, this feature helps reduce the operational burden of manually escalating invoices. For procurement and finance leaders, it provides added confidence that important invoices are reviewed according to company policy.

By aligning invoice approvals with the management hierarchy, organizations can create a more reliable control framework while still supporting efficient invoice processing.

With Level-Based Approval for Supplier Invoice Workflows, organizations can better manage approval complexity while keeping processes clear, consistent, and aligned with business needs   

Within Configure Decision Tables, you can set management levels for additional approvers in the new Additional Approvers Based on Organizational Level decision table, using the Management Level of Additional Approvers fields, up to three levels. The screenshot below shows these fields.

Then, during variant configuration, you can set the Approvers Based on Organizational Level option for the Additional Approvers field so that the system checks the decision table and assigns the required approvers.             

4.  Enhancements to Approval Task Assignment Reasons in My Inbox (CIM-3644)

More Clarity for Approval Tasks in My Inbox

Approvals are a critical step in the invoicing process. When approvers understand why a task is assigned to them, they can act faster, reduce follow-up questions, and help keep invoice processing moving.

With this release, SAP Ariba Invoicing introduces enhancements to approval task reasons assigned to approvers giving them more context directly where they work.

What’s New

With this feature, approvers can now see additional details in My Inbox about:

  • The type of approval task assigned to them
  • The channel through which they were assigned to the approval task

This added information helps approvers better understand the reason they received a specific invoice approval task without needing to search or ask for clarification.

Why This Matters

In many organizations, invoice approvals involve different roles, rules, and assignment methods. An approver may receive a task because they are part of a cost center approval flow, because they were delegated the task, or because they are included through another approval channel.  When that context is not clear, it can slow down the process. By making assignment reasons more visible in My Inbox, SAP Ariba Invoicing helps improve transparency and efficiency in day-to-day approval work.

Key Benefits

Faster Decision-Making

  • Approvers can quickly understand why a task is assigned to them, helping them review and act on invoices with greater confidence.

Fewer Clarification Requests

  • With more assignment details available directly in My Inbox, approvers spend less time asking procurement, accounts payable, or system administrators why they received a task.

Improved Approval Transparency

  • Clearer task assignment information supports better governance by making the approval process easier to understand for business users.

Smoother Invoice Processing

  • When approvers can act faster and with more context, organizations can reduce delays and support more timely invoice approvals.

Business Value

This enhancement is designed to make the approval experience more intuitive and transparent. For accounts payable and procurement teams, it can help reduce process friction and improve invoice cycle times. For approvers, it provides the context they need to take action more efficiently.

SAP continues to invest in user experience improvements that simplify procurement and invoicing processes. Enhancements like this one help ensure that users have the right information at the right time, directly within their workflow.

entry.title: A Question from My Stylist: Will AI Change Technology, or Will Technology Change AI?
entry.content:
It started in a swivel chair when my hair stylist paused mid-trim and asked me: “So, do you think AI will change technology, or will technology change AI? And what are the long-term impacts, really?”

I loved the question because it cuts to the heart of what so many of us are feeling about AI: excitement, curiosity, and maybe some unease. My answer, though, is simple. We’ve been here before. Not with AI, but with other inventions that felt like they might unravel us, until they didn’t. Instead, they extended what we could do.

Here’s what I told her.

First, I talked about calculators in schools and how initially teachers, principals, and superintendents worried that relying on them would stop students from learning math. That response came from a place of genuine concern, but over time we learned that calculators don’t erase mathematical thinking—they accelerate it. They move students past tedious steps to advanced concepts, freeing them to focus on the why and how rather than getting bogged down in mechanics. Calculators didn’t replace math; they reframed what we could do with it.

Then I talked about the internet, which wasn’t immediately welcomed in schools or places of work. In fact, many viewed it as a distraction or something superficial. Today, of course, we can’t imagine our jobs or our lives without it. The internet didn’t just give us information; it gave us velocity. And in procurement specifically, the results are concrete and measurable. We research suppliers, compare credentials, negotiate across time zones, and verify sustainability commitments online with a level of accuracy and speed that wasn’t possible before.

I believe AI will follow a similar path to both of these examples.

So, when my stylist asked whether AI will change technology or technology will change AI—my honest answer was yes to both. It’s a feedback loop. New AI capabilities inspire new tools, workflows, and platforms; advances in infrastructure expand what AI can do in return. Each nudges the other forward. But what matters most is how people like you and me put these tools to work in everyday contexts.

In procurement, with SAP’s Autonomous Spend Management solutions, this looks like:

  • Drafting contracts with Procurement Contract Assistant, where AI proposes clauses aligned to your risk appetite and flags exceptions for legal review before a human touches the document.
  • Using Sourcing Assistant to draw on prior contracts and past event data to build the RFx, scoring incoming bids against live risk signals and market benchmarks, then generating negotiation strategies—so you don’t have to start from scratch each round. The result is faster cycle times and more disciplined negotiations.
  • Making every supplier conversation more substantive through Supplier Management Assistant, which brings together fragmented data like the supplier’s performance history, financial health indicators, ESG signals, and collaboration records into a coherent picture.
  • Streamlining day-to-day purchasing with Requisition Assistant, which routes employees to the right buying channel, fills in the routine fields, and surfaces alternatives when requested items aren’t in the catalog. Spending stays on policy, people get what they need, and neither outcome requires anyone to become a procurement expert.

Each of these examples puts people at the helm with far better tools than they had before.

 My stylist asked if we should be worried about AI risks, and I told her: cautious, yes, but not paralyzed. Here’s what I meant.

The long-term impacts of AI are simple but profound:

  • We’ll shift from manual to meaningful. Just as calculators freed us from mathematical basics and the internet freed us from the card catalog at the library, AI will increasingly free us from repetitive digital labor, including reformatting data, summarizing documents, and reconciling routine discrepancies. That doesn't diminish our roles. It elevates them.
  • Skills will evolve, not evaporate. The worry that “if we use AI, we'll forget how to think” echoes the old calculator debate. But history consistently shows that automating lower-level tasks raises the ceiling for what’s possible. In procurement, that means learning to ask better questions of data, interpret AI-suggested scenarios, and orchestrate increasingly complex supplier ecosystems.
  • Speed won’t replace discernment. If the internet taught us anything, it’s that faster access to information actually heightens the need for critical thinking. AI will be no different. The best outcomes will come from teams that pair AI’s speed with human sense-making, ethics, and accountability. We still decide what “good” looks like.
  • Governance will mature alongside capability. Just as the internet required new norms around privacy, security, and digital literacy, AI demands guardrails like responsible data usage, transparency about model limitations, and clear lines of accountability. Getting this right isn’t optional; it's the foundation for trust and adoption.

My stylist listened closely—she always does—and agreed that life had played out that way with calculators and the internet. Then she finished my blow-dry and when I looked in the mirror, I realized my hair was shorter than I wanted. I immediately likened it to an AI prompt. I should have been more specific when she asked how much I wanted her to trim. The quality of what you get out is directly tied to the clarity of what you put in. That’s as true in the salon as it is in any system.

We each have a real opportunity to lean into what’s possible with AI - for today and tomorrow. To learn more about how SAP can support your procurement team with the process, join us at Spend Connect in Las Vegas October 5-7. Live and virtual sessions will be available.

entry.title: Guided Buying — Design Principles and Adoption
entry.content:
The Launch That Reversed Itself (An illustrative example)

Hannah, Procurement Transformation Manager at a Nordic energy company, launched guided buying with 94 per cent of the procurement team trained, 2,300 catalogue items loaded, and automated approval routing for routine purchases. Three months after go-live, non-PO invoice volume was down 38 per cent. Six months later it was creeping back up. By month nine it had reached 28 per cent of indirect transactions — almost exactly where it had started. When she investigated, the pattern was consistent: empty searches had risen steadily since launch. The items requesters most commonly needed were not in the catalogue — maintenance parts, local services, and vendors added to the approved supplier list after the initial content load but never reflected in the guided buying environment. The technology was working exactly as designed. The catalogue was not. A guided buying system whose content is static is, within twelve months, a system whose users have learned to go around it.

The Business Challenge

Guided buying is a company’s internal purchasing system — the interface employees use to order through approved suppliers and pre-agreed catalogue items. When it works, it routes spend toward contracted sources before purchases happen outside the system. The most common failure is a stale catalogue: content loaded at go-live and not maintained. When the catalogue no longer reflects what people actually need, they bypass it. Empty searches are the early warning: a rising empty-search rate typically precedes off-contract purchasing by four to six weeks.

The second failure mode is the opposite: overuse of hard blocks — mandatory rejection screens that prevent submission until a justification is provided. When hard blocks appear on every non-catalogue request, employees route around the system entirely, using corporate cards and expense claims instead. Those channels sit outside any spending record. Blocking one route while leaving others open moves the problem; it does not solve it.

Five Design Principles

Guided buying environments that sustain compliance over time share five design characteristics. They are not technology features — they are design decisions made before the platform is configured.

The Measurement Architecture

Login counts and training completion tell you whether people are accessing the system — not whether it is working. A programme can show high adoption while a third of all searches return nothing, meaning users are present but the catalogue is not serving them. The four metrics below measure effectiveness rather than activity. All four share one denominator: addressable spend — the portion of indirect expenditure the programme is designed to manage, not total organisational spend, which includes categories never within scope.

These four metrics move in a predictable sequence. Empty Search Rate rises first — when the catalogue stops serving real demand, typically four to six weeks before off-contract purchases appear in invoice data. Exception Volume by Category shows what demand the system cannot currently serve. PO Coverage Rate is the lagging measure: it moves last and can appear healthy while the other three are already deteriorating. Preferred Supplier Utilisation measures the depth of contract compliance — whether negotiated deals are being used, not simply whether purchases flow through the system.

Desired Outcomes

  • The guided buying environment is reviewed on a ninety-day catalogue refresh cycle. Empty search rate is tracked as a KPI and reported monthly; a rate above eight per cent triggers a catalogue gap review, not a user-training programme.
  • Progressive controls are applied by risk tier. Hard blocks are reserved for policy-violating or restricted transactions. Routine off-catalogue requests trigger a justification prompt, not a rejection.
  • Exception volume by category is reviewed quarterly. Categories with consistent non-catalogue demand have a sourcing response scheduled or in progress.

Maturity Benchmark

“Organisations that implement guided buying and actively manage catalogue completeness — on a ninety-day refresh cycle rather than an annual or event-driven basis — reduce maverick spend from a median of 31 per cent to under nine per cent of total indirect spend within twenty-four months. Those that treat the initial content load as a one-time exercise see compliance rates return to pre-implementation levels within twelve months, regardless of adoption statistics."
— Hackett Group, Procurement Performance Benchmark, 2023

Perspectives by Role

SAP and SAP Ariba — Relevant Context

SAP Ariba Buying provides the guided buying infrastructure this chapter describes. The environment is configured by buying category, persona, and legal entity, enabling differentiated experiences for different user groups. The platform’s Usage Report surfaces empty search rate, catalogue search volume, cart conversion rate, and approval cycle times as native analytics. Catalogue content connects to SAP Business Network for real-time pricing from contracted suppliers.

SAP S/4HANA closes the transaction loop: PO coverage rate, non-PO invoice volume, and off-contract spend by cost centre are measurable from transactional data. Exception workflows are configured by category and spend threshold. Together with SAP Ariba Buying, it provides the single-front-door, full-audit-trail architecture guided buying requires.

Key Takeaways

  • Guided buying solves maverick spend at the point of intent — but only if the catalogue reflects current demand. A catalogue loaded once at go-live and not maintained is a guided buying implementation in name only.
  • Empty searches are the leading indicator of compliance erosion. They appear four to six weeks before off-contract purchasing re-emerges in invoice data. Track them as a control metric, not a user-experience issue.
  • Hard stops on every non-standard request train users to route around the system. Progressive controls — information prompt, then warning with justification, then block — sustain adoption where hard gates erode it.
  • Measure guided buying effectiveness on PO coverage rate, empty search rate, preferred supplier utilisation, and exception volume — not on training completion or login counts. Login counts are exposure metrics: they confirm access, not outcomes. Only the four operational measures show whether maverick spend is actually declining.
  • Guided buying is not a project with a go-live date — it is a product with named owners, regular search log reviews, and continuous improvement cycles. Environments treated as finished after launch erode within twelve months. The organisations that sustain compliance gains are those that fund ongoing product ownership, not just the initial implementation.

References

entry.title: SAP Ariba Procure to Order 2608 Release Key Innovations
entry.content:
Hello SAP Ariba Community, and welcome to our 2608 Key Innovations blog.

This release brings several user-focused enhancements across Buying and Procurement core processes, helping organisations improve compliance, streamline approvals, and make purchasing decisions with greater confidence.

Attachments now included in Requisition Approval Emails (PROC-1115)

SAP Ariba Buying Approvers can now receive header and line-level requisition attachments directly within approval email notifications. This means supporting documents such as quotes, specifications, and statements of work can be reviewed without needing to log in to SAP Ariba.

Why it matters
Providing key documents directly in approval emails gives approvers more context when making decisions and can help speed up approval turnaround times.

Who will benefit?

  • Approvers (especially those non desk-based approvers)
  • Procurement teams
  • Organisations that rely on supporting documentation during approvals

Setup Requirements

  • Enable the Include attachments in requisition approval email notifications parameter.

 

 

Improved Search for Purchase Requisitions in Your Approvals (GUIDEB-1343)

A new Requisitions tab in Your Approvals provides enhanced search and filtering options, making it easier for approvers to find requisitions waiting for action.

Available filters include Requisition ID, title, supplier, last updated date, requester, and request type.

Why it matters
Approvers can more quickly find relevant requisitions, particularly in organisations with high approval volumes or large multi-line requisitions.

Who will benefit?

  • Managers and approvers
  • Shared services teams
  • Procurement approvers

Setup Requirements

  • Enable Guided Buying parameter PARAM_ENABLE_APPROVAL_FILTERS = true.

Additional Considerations When enabled, requisitions awaiting approval appear in the new Requisitions tab rather than the traditional To Approve tab.

 

Procurement Transfer of Ownership API (PROC-1129)

This new API enables organisations to transfer ownership of purchase requisitions, purchase orders, and associated receipts from one user to another within SAP Ariba Buying. This is particularly valuable when employees leave the business or move into new roles and organisations can be left with many documents in a state of limbo.

Why it matters
The API helps maintain business continuity by ensuring procurement documents remain actively managed and do not become tied to inactive users.

Who will benefit?

  • Procurement operations teams
  • System administrators
  • IT teams managing SAP Ariba integrations

Setup Requirements

  • Enable Application.Procure.OpenApiForTooEnabled
  • Enable Application.TransferOwnershipRequest.Enabled
  • Access to the SAP Ariba Developer Portal is required
  • OAuth authentication must be configured

Additional Considerations This enhancement is primarily relevant for technical and administrative teams rather than end users.

 

Enhanced Supplier Search for RFQs in Guided Buying (GUIDEB-1194)

Users creating RFQs in Guided Buying can now search a wider supplier base using the new View All Suppliers option. Previously, RFQs were limited to qualified or preferred suppliers only. This is of course is an optional capability to bring in more flexibility, where some organisations will want to restrict to qualified or preferred suppliers only.

The enhanced search experience includes additional filtering and sorting capabilities and can return up to 200 suppliers.

Why it matters
Expanding supplier visibility can improve competition, increase sourcing options, and help users identify the most suitable suppliers for their requirements.

Who will benefit?

  • Sourcing teams
  • Procurement teams
  • Business users creating RFQs

Setup Requirements

  • Enable PARAM_ENABLE_ENHANCED_SUPPLIER_SEARCH
  • Enable PARAM_ENABLE_VIEW_ALL_SUPPLIERS_IN_RFQ = true

Additional Considerations Both parameters must be enabled for the new functionality to be available.

 

Increased Controls for Purchase Order Changes (GUIDEB-1352)

Organisations can now prevent users who created a Guided Buying requisition, from changing, cancelling, or deleting the associated purchase order after it reaches Ordered status.

When enabled, users who submitted the original requisition will no longer see the Cancel Request, Change Request, or Delete options once the order has been placed.

Why it matters
This helps strengthen procurement controls, reduce accidental order changes, and minimise disruption to supplier relationships after orders have been placed.

Who will benefit?

  • Procurement governance teams
  • Purchasing teams
  • Organisations with stricter compliance requirements

Setup Requirements

  • Enable Guided Buying parameter PARAM_ENABLE_RESTRICTION_OF_CANCELLATION = true

 

 

Restrict On-Behalf-Of Plant Selection to a User's Company Code (GUIDEB-1350)

For organisations using Request by Plant function in Guided Buying, this enhancement helps ensure users can only select plants that are relevant to their own company code. Previously, users could see and select plants outside their company code, potentially leading to incorrect plant assignments or the selection of items and suppliers that were not valid for their organisation.

When enabled, the plant selection list is automatically filtered so users only see plants associated with their company code.

Why it matters
This enhancement helps improve purchasing accuracy, reduces the risk of incorrect plant assignments, and supports better compliance with organisational procurement structures.

Who will benefit?

  • Organisations operating across multiple company codes and plants
  • Requisitioners using Request by Plant
  • Procurement teams seeking stronger purchasing controls

Setup Requirements

  • Enable Guided Buying parameter PARAM_ENABLE_PLANT_PORG_RESTRICTION_BY_COMPANY_CODE = true
  • Users purchasing on behalf of other users, company codes, purchasing units, or plants must have team buying disabled.
  • If required, administrators can disable team buying using PARAM_ENABLE_TEAM_BUYING.

entry.title: Purchase Order Management
entry.content:
The Invoice That Preceded the Order

Marcus Lund, Procurement Operations Manager at a regional infrastructure firm, opened the quarterly AP report to find that 31 per cent of invoices in the period had been processed without a matched purchase order. Each had required manual resolution. The invoices were legitimate; the spend had been authorised by budget holders; the suppliers had delivered. The problem was not what was purchased. It was when the authorisation occurred.

The purchase order is procurement’s primary operational control. It converts a sourcing decision into a formal, authorised commitment: it specifies the supplier, goods or services, quantity, agreed price, and delivery terms before any obligation is incurred. The PO is the reference document against which goods receipt and supplier invoice are both verified. Without it, the three-way match — the verification mechanism that closes the loop between commitment, delivery, and payment — has no anchor.

In standard procurement practice, the purchase order does not originate directly from a business need — it is preceded by a purchase requisition (PR): an internal document raised by the requesting department that specifies what is needed, at what estimated cost, and by when. The requisition passes through internal approval — budget check, demand justification, and authority confirmation — and only once formally approved does procurement convert it into a purchase order for transmission to the supplier. The approved PR is the authorisation record: no purchase order should be raised without a corresponding approved requisition. Bypassing the PR and committing informally to a supplier is precisely the mechanism that produces retrospective POs: the obligation exists before the system has recorded any authorisation for it.

 

The Business Challenge

 

PO Matching — Why It Saves Money, and How Much

The Aberdeen Group publishes annual benchmarks on accounts payable (AP) processing efficiency. Their research measures the full cost of handling one supplier invoice from receipt to payment — including staff time, system costs, exception handling, and query resolution. Their benchmark shows a consistent cost gap between two invoice types:

 

 

The most common failure in PO management is not fraud — it is timing. Goods arrive before the approval is complete. A requester agrees to a purchase verbally, then creates the PO afterwards just to close the system record. At that point, the document is recording a decision that has already been made, not authorising one that is about to be. The PO exists on paper; the control never operated. Organisations should track retrospective PO volume as a separate metric from overall PO coverage, because the two numbers measure entirely different things.

PO quality also affects the supplier relationship. Suppliers who receive clear, complete POs — with accurate specifications, agreed pricing, and confirmed delivery details — can plan their work and deliver on time. Suppliers who receive vague or frequently changed POs face extra administration, cannot plan reliably, and often wait longer to be paid. Procurement then has to handle those payment delays as disputes. Getting the PO right at the start reduces problems at every stage that follows.

Approval Workflow Design

Both observations point toward the same lever. The quality of what the PO contains at creation and the structure of the approval workflow that precedes it are not separate management problems — they are two expressions of the same underlying challenge: designing the authorisation process so that the controlled path is also the efficient path. An approval architecture that is too slow or too uniform pushes requestors toward informal commitment, which produces retrospective POs, which arrive at the match stage carrying incomplete data, which generates exceptions. Each failure in the chain traces to the same source.

The approval workflow determines whether the PO controls commitment before spend occurs or ratifies it after. Effective workflow design applies the lightest control that adequately addresses the transaction risk. Routine catalogue purchases from approved suppliers at pre-agreed prices warrant automated clearance; a high-value, non-contract engagement with a new supplier warrants structured review. When every transaction carries the same approval burden regardless of risk, the formal route becomes slower than informal commitment — and informal commitment wins. Compliance by design means the control architecture makes the compliant path the fastest path, not a competing one.

 

Desired Outcomes

  • PO coverage rates reflect genuine pre-commitment authorisation. Retrospective PO volume is tracked as a separate metric alongside the overall PO coverage rate.
  • Approval workflows are calibrated by financial value and risk category so that the compliant path is also the fastest path for routine purchases.
  • Three-way match exception rates fall because PO data quality improvements at creation reduce the administrative disputes that manual invoice processing generates.

Maturity Benchmark

“Organisations that sustain pre-commitment PO rates above 90 per cent report exception rates less than half those operating below 70 per cent. The gap is explained not by enforcement effort but by process design.
— Aberdeen Group, Procurement Benchmark, 2023

A mature process executes predefined controls consistently and routes only meaningful exceptions to human reviewers — eliminating routine handling without removing the controls themselves.

Perspectives by Role

How SAP Ariba Buying puts the chapter’s principles into practice

SAP Ariba Buying is the primary interface through which purchase requisitions are raised and routed for approval. The guided buying experience enforces compliance at the point of request: requestors see catalogue items from contracted suppliers first; non-catalogue requests require additional justification before submission; and eligibility rules are applied automatically. A request that does not meet the configured criteria cannot proceed without an explicit override — so every PR arrives in the approval queue already screened against policy. The Maverick spend percentage — the share of spend placed outside contracted channels — is the standard metric for measuring guided-buying adoption. SAP Ariba Buying surfaces this via its spend analytics: a rising off-contract or non-catalogue share signals gaps in catalogue coverage or systematic bypass of the guided channel.

Approval workflows are fully configurable by spending category, supplier type, cost centre, and transaction value. Threshold-based routing rules direct low-value catalogue purchases to auto-approval, route non-catalogue spend to line manager approval, and escalate high-value or non-contract transactions to dual sign-off from Procurement and Finance. This is compliance by design: the system encodes the three-tier approval architecture described in this chapter and triggers the correct route automatically rather than by individual judgement.

What a completed purchase order looks like in SAP Ariba Buying:

 

Purchase Order in SAP Ariba Next Generation Buying
 
Once the PR clears the approval workflow in SAP Ariba Buying, it is transferred to SAP S/4HANA, where a Purchaser creates the purchase order. The confirmed PO is shared back into Ariba Buying via the Purchase Order Collaboration integration — which is why it appears in the Ariba Buying “Purchase Orders” view, as the screenshot shows — and transmitted electronically to the supplier via SAP Business Network. Goods receipt is also processed in S/4HANA, with references fed back to Ariba to keep the requisition record complete.
 
Artificial intelligence is being applied across the purchase order lifecycle at the points where manual judgement currently creates the most friction: deciding which requisitions need human review, structuring free-form purchase requests into policy-compliant documents, and surfacing real-time visibility into approval queues and spend commitments. In each case the value of AI is not to remove the control but to reduce the cost of operating it — making the authorisation process fast enough that the compliant path is genuinely the most convenient path, which is the condition under which retrospective PO creation becomes unnecessary rather than merely discouraged.

Joule in SAP Ariba Solutions

SAP’s AI copilot Joule is confirmed as available within SAP Ariba Solutions, providing natural language interaction with procurement data and workflows. According to SAP’s published one-pager, Joule enhances productivity through faster informational searches and execution of navigation tasks, with user-friendly, natural language guided interfaces. In a procurement context, this means a requisitioner or approver can query approval queue status, open purchase orders, or spend commitment in natural language rather than navigating reports manually. The productivity benefit is real; the design boundary remains the same as for any AI capability: Joule supports navigation and information retrieval, it does not replace the human judgement behind an approval decision.

Key Takeaways

  • The purchase order is procurement’s primary operational control. Raised before the obligation is incurred, it authorises budget, binds commercial terms, and creates the reference document for verification and payment. A purchase requisition (PR) precedes every PO as the internal authorisation gate; bypassing it produces retrospective commitments that undermine the control entirely.
  • Your overall PO coverage rate shows what proportion of invoices had a purchase order attached. It does not show whether that PO was raised before or after the commitment was made. A PO created after goods have already been ordered still counts towards your coverage figure — but it provided no control over the spend. Tracking retrospective POs as a separate number shows how much of your apparent coverage reflects genuine advance authorisation, and how much is simply paperwork completed after the event.
  • Effective approval design is compliance by design — it prevents non-compliant spend by making the controlled path the fastest path. Apply the lightest control that adequately addresses the transaction risk: automated clearance for catalogue purchases, structured review for high-value or non-contract transactions.

References

  1. Aberdeen Group. 2023. Accounts Payable Automation: The Business Case for PO-Based Invoicing. Boston: Aberdeen.
  2. Hackett Group. 2023. Procurement Performance Benchmark. Miami: The Hackett Group.
  3. Ardent Partners. 2023. ePayables 2023: Transformation Continues in Accounts Payable. Boston: Ardent Partners.
  4. Lysons, Kenneth, and Brian Farrington. 2016. Procurement and Supply Chain Management. 9th ed. Harlow: Pearson Education.
  5. CIPS. 2022. Purchasing and Supply Management. Stamford: Chartered Institute of Procurement & Supply.

entry.title: Connected by Design: Run Integrated Business Processes, Out of the Box
entry.content:
Running a business well depends on connected processes working together across the organization. A customer opportunity can flow seamlessly through to revenue recognition, a purchase request can move smoothly through to supplier payment, and a workforce plan can connect a hiring decision to a productive employee. Finance and human resources (HR) shape many of these outcomes, giving both functions a unique opportunity to turn connected processes and data into better decisions for the entire business.

 

The strategic question Finance and HR can answer together

Finance and HR often approach the same business opportunity from two complementary angles. Finance brings a cost and capacity lens: how licensing, integration, and infrastructure decisions translate into what the organization can actually execute on. HR brings a focus on agility and the ability to launch initiatives like a new onboarding cycle as the business requires. Bringing those perspectives together opens up a better question: What becomes possible when Finance and HR work from a real-time, intelligent view of the business?

Each system reflected the priorities, requirements, and possibilities of the moment in which it was selected. As the business evolved, those individual choices created an opportunity to bring together what had previously been managed separately. It's no longer a question of whether each system works on its own, but how Finance and HR can build on those investments to create a shared foundation for the decisions they increasingly need to make together.

 

When Finance and HR work from the same context

The organizations leading this shift tend to have one thing in common. They're organizing workforce strategy around a single source of insight rather than around separate functional perspectives. When those workflows connect, the data they produce isn't Finance's version and HR's version sitting side by side. It's one shared picture, built on the same definitions from the start. Connected workflows give Finance and HR the context to evaluate priorities, respond to change, and give leaders a stronger basis for timely, confident decisions.

That shared approach turns integration into everyday business value. Workforce planning becomes a continuous exchange between Finance and HR, while scenario modeling gives CFOs and CHROs something they can act on, not just present. Compliance becomes easier to manage, and smoother handoffs across hiring, onboarding, and budgeting help the organization move forward with greater speed and confidence.

The result is a different kind of conversation. Finance and HR can spend less time establishing context and more time evaluating options, setting priorities, and acting together. Alignment becomes the starting point rather than the outcome.

 

How SAP-managed public cloud ERP turns connection into business value

Across our customer conversations, one thing kept coming up: customers want to focus on business outcomes from day one, with the applications and integrations ready to support them.

SAP-managed public cloud ERP provides that foundation, connecting business processes and data so that teams can work efficiently across functions and turn shared insight into coordinated action. When a customer selects a business scenario like Workforce Management, the integration comes out of the box. SAP provisions all required applications and integration in one guided experience, keeping technical decisions to a minimum and taking care of monitoring and operations. Customers and partners implement the full scenario together, and partners go straight to business design and the outcomes that matter most to customers. Workforce Management (SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition and SAP SuccessFactors Employee Central) and Operational Procurement (SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition and SAP Ariba Buying and Invoicing) are both running in Early Adopter phase now. The next scenario is Opportunity to Order (SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition and SAP Sales Cloud V2).

The SAP-managed public cloud ERP community is where you can get the full picture on the latest scenarios, the Early Adopter Care program, as well as blog posts, webinars, and opportunities to learn from customers and partners making the same shift. Connect with us there to ask questions and explore how to get involved or find more under the tag "SAP-managed Public Cloud ERP". If this post sparked a question or an idea, continue the conversation in the comments.
